SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. If
you need a refresher on this procedure, see Appendix A, "Standard Project Setup
Procedure."
■ Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Space SHMUP Part 1
■ Starter UnityPackage: Find Chapter 31 at http://book.prototools.net
■ Scene Name: ( __Scene_0 is included in the import)
■ Project Folders: __Scripts (two underscores before "Scripts") and
_Prefabs
■ Game Pane Dimensions: (will be set in the chapter)
■ Rename: (_MainCamera is included in the imported __Scene_0)
Importing a Unity Asset Package
One new thing in the setup for this prototype is that you must download and import
a custom Unity asset package. The creation of complex art and imagery for games is
beyond the scope of this book, but I've created a package of some fantastic starships by
Peter Burroughs
1
as well as other assets that will allow you to create all the visual effects
required for this game. Of course, as mentioned several times throughout this book, when
you're making a prototype, how it plays and feels are much more important than how it
looks, but having an understanding of how to work with art assets is still important.
The instructions for downloading and installing a Starter UnityPackage as required for
this chapter are in Appendix A, "Standard Project Setup Procedure." Follow those to
import the IGDPD3e.C31_Space_SHMUP_Starter.unitypackage for this chapter. The
Import Unity Package window for this chapter is shown in Figure 31.2a.
1. To learn more about Peter's work, check out his website at https://kairosmith.com/.

Select all the files as shown in Figure 31.2a (by clicking the All button), and click Import.
This imports a __Scene_0, places four new textures and one new shader into the
_Materials folder, and includes many models, textures, and other assets in the Assets by

Textures are usually just image files. The creation of textures is beyond the scope of this
book, but many books and online tutorials cover texture creation. Adobe Photoshop is
probably the most commonly used image editing tool, but it is very expensive. A com-
mon open source alternative is Gimp (http://www.gimp.org), and a good new com-
mercial competitor is Affinity Photo (https://affinity.serif.com/photo). By far, the easiest
image editor to access is Photopea (pronounced Photo-pee), which is an entirely free
online tool that reproduces most of the capabilities of Photoshop in a web browser. You
can find it at https://www.photopea.com/.

The creation of shaders is also far beyond the scope of this book. Shaders are programs
that tell your computer how to render a texture on a GameObject. They can make a
scene look realistic, cartoony, or however else you like, and they are an important part

elements that you want to be a specific bright color, this custom UnlitAlpha shader is
perfect. We'll use UnlitAlpha for the power-up cubes in this game (and differentiate it

chunks.content:
INPUT AXES AND THE INPUT MANAGER
Much of the code in the Hero.8pdate() code listing should look familiar to you,
though this is the first time in the book that you've seen the Input.Get$[is()
method. Unity's Input Manager allows you to configure various input axes, and
those axes can be read through Input.Get$[is(). To view the default Input axes,
choose Edit > Project Settings… from the menu bar and then choose Input Manager
from the left sidebar. You will probably need to click the disclosure triangle next to
Axes to show all of them, as shown in Figure 31.4.
Figure 31.4 Unity's Input Manager showing the default Horizontal axis settings (split in two
halves; the first for keyboard, and the second for joystick)
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
makInG the hero shIP 763
One thing to note about the settings in Figure 31.4 is that several axis names are
listed twice (e.g., Horizontal, Vertical, and Jump). As you can see in the expanded
view of the two Horizontal axes in the figure, this allows the Horizontal axis to be
controlled by either presses on the keyboard (accepting left and right arrow as
well as A and D, as shown in the left image of Figure 31.4) or a joystick axis (shown
in the right image). This is one of the great strengths of the input axes; several
different types of input can control a single axis. As a result, your games only need
one line to read the value of an axis rather than a line to handle joystick input, a
line for each arrow key, and a line each for the A and D keys.
Every call to Input.Get$[is() returns a float between − 1 and 1 in value (with
a default of 0). Each axis in the Input Manager also includes values for Sensitivity
and Gravity, though these are only used for Key or Mouse Button input (see the left
image of Figure 31.4). Sensitivity and Gravity cause the axis value to interpolate
smoothly when a key is pressed or released. (That is, instead of immediately jump-
ing to the final value, the axis value will blend from the original value to the final
value over time.) In the Horizontal axis shown, a sensitivity of 3 means that when
the right-arrow key is pressed, it takes 1/3 of a second for the value to interpolate
from 0 to 1. A gravity of 3 means that when the right-arrow key is released, it takes
1/3 of a second for the axis value to interpolate back to 0. The higher the sensitiv-
ity or gravity, the faster the interpolation takes place.
The effect of the Snap setting is subtle but important. When Snap is false (unchecked),
if the Horizontal axis is currently − 1 (i.e., fully left), and you press and hold the right
arrow key, the value will smoothly interpolate back to 0 and then to 1. On the other
hand, when Snap is true (the default), if the Horizontal axis is currently − 1, and you

As with many things in Unity, you can find out a lot more about the Input Man-

at making input consistent across several brands of game pads (e.g., Microsoft,
Sony, Nintendo), it takes much more effort to configure and is not needed for the
keyboard and mouse input used throughout this book.

Part of what makes this feel nice is the apparent inertia that the ship carries. When you

Chapter 26, "Classes," covered a bit about the Enemy class and subclasses for a game
like this. There you learned about setting up a superclass for all enemies that can be
extended by its subclasses. For this game, you will extend that further in the next
chapter, but first, let's create the artwork.
Enemy Artwork
The hero has a very warm gold tone, so to contrast this, the enemies were modeled
with cool blues and purples. Enemies are also round to contrast with the hero ship's
more angular aesthetic. You can see all five enemies in Figure 31.5, though we'll only
implement Enemy_0 in this chapter.
Figure 31.5 Each of the five enemy ship types
Preparing Enemy_0 for the game is very similar to the process you used to get _Hero
ready, though we'll do it in a slightly different order:
1. Create an empty GameObject named Enemy_0.
a. Choose GameObject > Create Empty from the Unity menu.
b. Rename the GameObject to Enemy_0.
c. Set the Enemy_0 transform to P:[ 0, 20, 0 ], R:[ 0, 0, 0 ], S:[ 1.5, 1.5, 1.5 ].

0.01, 0.01 ].
Now, we need to add the components that will allow this enemy to work in the game.
All of these will be attached to the Enemy_0 root-level GameObject, not to its enemy0
child.
3. Select Enemy_0 at the root level of the Hierarchy and add a Capsule Collider.
a. Double-click Enemy_0 in the Hierarchy to focus on it in the Scene view. You may
want to click the 2D button at the top of the Scene view to view Enemy_0 from
the same orientation as the orthographic _MainCamera.
b. With Enemy_0 selected, click the Add Component button and add a Capsule Col-
lider (you can find it under Physics > or by typing "Capsule" into the search bar).
c. Set the Capsule Collider Radius to 1.2.
d. Set the Capsule Collider Height to 2.9.
You should see that the Capsule Collider now completely surrounds Enemy_0. There is
some empty space within the Capsule Collider, but a good thing to remember is that
players will be much more upset if they think they hit an enemy but the shot didn't
register than if they think they missed but the shot did register, so it's always better for
enemies to err on the side of making the colliders for enemies too large. On the other
hand, for the player themselves, they'll rarely complain if they think they were probably
supposed to get hit, but the game doesn't count it. So always make your colliders for
the player smaller or make it very clear where the boundary is (as we've done with the
circular shield).

If an enum has the >SysteP.)lags@ compiler attribute, then it will be able to
hold multiple values at the same time. >SysteP.)lags@ enums are also some-
times called bitmasks because you can think of each binary bit (i.e., an individual 0
or 1 in a variable) in the enum as representing a single value being true or false.
For example, the /ayerMasN type in Unity is a >SysteP.)lags@ enum, with each
of the binary bits of the 32-bit enum representing one of the 32 possible Lay-
ers being enabled or disabled. You can see this by selecting _MainCamera in the
scene Hierarchy and looking in the Camera component of the Inspector at the Cull-

you can also individually turn Layers on and off because the /ayerMasN culling
MasN is a Flags enum.
The >SysteP.)lags@ enuP eScreen/ocs will work in a similar way. The value
of each of the defined off screen positions is a different power of 2, as shown in
Figure 31.7b. Because these are powers of 2 (i.e., 0, 1, 2, 4, & 8), they each can be
represented by a single bit in the enum.

Setting Tags, Layers, and Physics
As was presented in Chapter 29, " Apple Picker," one of the things that layers control in
Unity is which objects do or do not collide with each other. First, let's think about the
Space SHMUP prototype. In this game, several different types of GameObjects could be
placed on five distinct layers that will interact with each other in different ways:
■ Hero: The _Hero ship should collide with enemies, enemy projectiles, and power-
ups but should not collide with hero projectiles.
■ Enemy: Enemies should collide with _Hero and hero projectiles but not with
power-ups.
■ ProjectileHero: Projectiles fired by _Hero should only collide with enemies.

couple things about the Bézier curve movement:

ever makes it all the way down to the bottom of the screen. This happens

move down quickly, then slow and move back upward without ever touching
the bottom of the screen.

sometimes a curse) of the math that makes Bézier curves work. The individual
points of a Bézier curve are spaced further apart at the endpoints and much
closer together in the middle.

A Generic Dictionary for WeaponDefinitions
To make accessing the :eaponDefinitions easier, you're going to copy them at
runtime from the ZeaponDefinitions array to a static priYate Dictionary field
named :E$PBDI&T. A Dictionary is a type of generic collection like /ist. However,
where a /ist is an ordered (linear) collection, each entry in a Dictionary has both a
key and a value, with the key used to retrieve the value. Dictionaries can be a good way
to store a very large number of things because accessing any one of those things is a
constant time operation, meaning that it takes the same small amount of time regard-
less of where that thing is in the data structure. Contrast this with a /ist or array; if
you were searching through the ZeaponDefinitions array for the :eaponDefinition
with the type blaster, you would encounter it immediately, whereas searching for the
:eaponDefinition with the type shield would take three times as long.
